title: Make the comparison visible.
dek: When presenting several numbers, decide which comparison the audience should make. Arrange or plot the values so that comparison is easy to see.

point: A table can contain all the relevant evidence while making the audience search for the relationship you want to discuss. title: Explain the question before the model.
dek: Introduce a model by explaining the economic question it will answer. The audience can then understand why its assumptions and equations are needed.

point: Before introducing a model’s formal structure, explain the behavior or outcome you want to understand and the difficulty the model will help resolve. As you introduce agents, constraints, and choices, connect them to that purpose. This gives listeners a reason to follow the setup and a way to judge which details matter.

dek: Define the symbols a listener needs on the slide where they are used. Explain what the expression says in economic terms.

point: Listeners may forget a definition or miss the moment when it is introduced. Put short definitions beside the expressions that depend on them, even if the notation appeared earlier. State what the calculation measures or what the equation says about economic behavior, so the audience can recover the argument while looking at the current slide.

title: Explain how to read the figure.
dek: Before presenting a complicated figure, explain what its lines, regions, or symbols mean. Teach one element at a time, then show how they fit together.
point: Reading a figure requires knowing what its visual elements represent. Introduce the axes and explain one curve, shaded region, or line style before asking the audience to interpret several together. Build toward the complete figure while keeping familiar elements in place, so each addition extends what listeners already understand.

title: Draw the uncertainty with the estimate.
dek: Display uncertainty alongside the estimates you discuss. A listener should be able to see both the estimated magnitude and how precisely it is measured.

point: Interpreting an estimate requires information about its precision. Plotting estimates with clearly labeled confidence intervals lets the audience see their magnitudes and uncertainty together, with the relevant reference value marked. title: Put the finding in the title.
dek: Use a results slide’s title to state the finding the audience should remember. Match the strength of that statement to what the evidence supports.

point: A results slide is easier to follow when listeners know which conclusion its evidence is meant to support. State that conclusion in a sentence at the top, then use the table or figure to substantiate it. Keep the wording precise about the population, comparison, and strength of inference, including whether the evidence establishes an association or a causal effect.

title: Start with the smallest useful example.
dek: Introduce a general model through a small example that preserves its central mechanism. Work through the example before explaining what carries over to the general case.

point: Choose a simple case in which the main economic force still operates. Work through the relevant choices, interactions, and outcome before presenting the general notation or result. Then explain which features carry over and which depend on the simplification. The example gives listeners a concrete argument to recognize in the more general analysis.

title: Trace one path before the full system.
dek: When a model has many connected parts, first trace one path from an input to an outcome. Add the other connections after the audience understands that path.

before.title: Two-asset HANK graph · PDF p. 72

Finance also takes \((p,d,r)\) from equity and \(i\) from monetary policy.
after.note: Equity values and monetary policy also enter the finance block.

after.label: HOUSEHOLD CHOICES

after.label: THE COMPLETE SYSTEM

diagnosis: The source moves from simpler models to a much richer two-asset graph. At this jump, the audience must decode seven blocks and twenty dependencies while also learning which paths are unknown and which conditions close the model.
changes: Identify the unknowns and equilibrium targets first.
Trace a short chain before following its branches.
Explain the household connections, then restore every original edge.
preserved: The complete source diagram returns unchanged in the final build: seven blocks, twenty labeled links, three unknown paths, and three equilibrium targets.
deferred: The first teaching panels show selected dependency groups. The full graph, including equity, monetary-policy, and direct fiscal connections, remains the destination.
practice: Choose one path through your most complicated diagram. Teach its inputs, intermediate objects, and destination before revealing the surrounding network.
context: NBER Summer Institute, July 2019. The authors already teach simpler directed graphs: a Krusell–Smith model on PDF p. 61 and a one-asset HANK model on p. 71. This revision adds a bridge into the two-asset graph on p. 72 (printed slide 24).
beforeCaption: Two-asset HANK: seven blocks, twenty dependencies, three equilibrium targets.
afterCaption: Four rebuilt views of the same model dependencies.

source.authors: Adrien Auclert, Bence Bardóczy, Matt Rognlie, Ludwig Straub
source.title: Using the Sequence-Space Jacobian to Solve and Estimate Heterogeneous-Agent Models

values: Source inputs: exogenous Z, r*, G; endogenous unknown paths r, w, Y.
Seven blocks: production, fiscal, price Phillips curve, equity, finance, monetary policy, and heterogeneous households.
Three targets: Fisher equation H1, asset market clearing H2, wage Phillips curve H3.
The source graph has twenty labeled directed connections. Its complete original appears in the final better build.
point: A diagram of an entire model can ask listeners to learn many relationships at once. Begin with one input, show what it affects next, and follow the chain to an outcome the audience cares about. Add the remaining branches and feedbacks in stages, explaining what each contributes, before returning to the complete system.

title: Explain what each limitation qualifies.
dek: Connect each limitation to the conclusion it affects. Explain how it changes what the audience can infer from the evidence or carry over to another setting.

Translate each caveat into a question about that result.
Keep the original response plot available with its full specification.

practice: Write “What this establishes” and “What it leaves open” in equally plain language. Check both with your advisor.

source.authors: Gilbert E. Metcalf, James H. Stock
source.title: The Macroeconomic Impact of Europe’s Carbon Taxes

values: The GDP-level response is replotted from the chart on PDF p. 25. Coordinates were digitized from its raster plot and are approximate.
The plot retains horizons 0–6, both 67% and 95% bands, and the zero line. The vertical axis is tightened to ±3 percentage points so the bands can be read.
The experiment is a $40 carbon-tax increase in real 2018 US dollars, weighted by coverage share. Sample EU+; restricted local projections; parallel-path assumption; four lags.
Approximate point estimates at years 0–6: 0.04, 0.13, 0.31, 0.29, −0.04, 0.08, 0.08 percentage points.
point: A limitation is informative when the audience understands its consequence for a claim. State the finding, identify the inference at issue, and explain how a remaining uncertainty or assumption restricts that inference. Distinguish questions about causal interpretation, precision, and applicability to other settings, so listeners understand both what the work establishes and what remains open.
